base_method_text.title:
The Stronger the Diffusion Model, the Easier the Backdoor: Data
  Poisoning to Induce Copyright Breaches Without Adjusting Finetuning Pipeline
base_method_text.summary:
The commercialization of text-to-image diffusion models (DMs) brings forth
potential copyright concerns. Despite numerous attempts to protect DMs from
copyright issues, the vulnerabilities of these solutions are underexplored. In
this study, we formalized the Copyright Infringement Attack on generative AI
models and proposed a backdoor attack method, SilentBadDiffusion, to induce
copyright infringement without requiring access to or control over training
processes. Our method strategically embeds connections between pieces of
copyrighted information and text references in poisoning data while carefully
dispersing that information, making the poisoning data inconspicuous when
integrated into a clean dataset. Our experiments show the stealth and efficacy
of the poisoning data. When given specific text prompts, DMs trained with a
poisoning ratio of 0.20% can produce copyrighted images. Additionally, the
results reveal that the more sophisticated the DMs are, the easier the success
of the attack becomes. These findings underline potential pitfalls in the
prevailing copyright protection strategies and underscore the necessity for
increased scrutiny to prevent the misuse of DMs.
base_method_text.main_contributions: The paper formalizes the Copyright Infringement Attack on generative AI models, proposing a backdoor attack method called SilentBadDiffusion. This method strategically embeds connections between copyrighted information and text references in poisoning data to induce copyright infringement in text-to-image diffusion models without adjusting the fine-tuning pipeline. The research demonstrates that more sophisticated DMs are more susceptible to this attack.
base_method_text.methodology: SilentBadDiffusion involves semantically dissecting a copyrighted image into elements and incorporating them into multiple images with corresponding text captions. This is achieved using a multi-modal large language model to identify salient parts of an image, a semantic segmentation model (GroundingDINO and SAM) to extract visual elements, and an inpainting model to create poisoning images. A Substantial Similarity Assessment Model (SSCD) is used to assess the similarity of the generated images.
base_method_text.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted using Stable Diffusion (SD) versions 1.1 to 1.5, fine-tuned on poisoned datasets. The Pokemon BLIP Captions dataset and subsets of LAION Aesthetics v2 6.5+ and COYO-700m datasets were used as clean datasets. Midjourney v5 data was used as copyrighted material. The effectiveness of the attack was measured by Copyright Infringement Rate (CIR) and First-Attack Epoch (FAE), with Self Supervised Copy Detection (SSCD) used to detect substantial similarity.
base_method_text.limitations: The approach assumes that copyright images are decomposable into distinct elements. The study acknowledges the potential for discrepancies between SSCD outcomes and human judgment in assessing substantial similarity. The method's effectiveness may vary depending on the specific architecture and training of the diffusion model.
base_method_text.future_research_directions: Future research could focus on a broader range of targets beyond decomposable images, leveraging optimization techniques to integrate copyright information by updating pixel-wise values of training data. Other areas include exploring style-attack and multiple-backdoors attack scenarios, as well as theoretical investigations into the memorization mechanisms of diffusion models.

add_method_texts.title:
TERD: A Unified Framework for Safeguarding Diffusion Models Against
  Backdoors
add_method_texts.summary:
Diffusion models have achieved notable success in image generation, but they
remain highly vulnerable to backdoor attacks, which compromise their integrity
by producing specific undesirable outputs when presented with a pre-defined
trigger. In this paper, we investigate how to protect diffusion models from
this dangerous threat. Specifically, we propose TERD, a backdoor defense
framework that builds unified modeling for current attacks, which enables us to
derive an accessible reversed loss. A trigger reversion strategy is further
employed: an initial approximation of the trigger through noise sampled from a
prior distribution, followed by refinement through differential multi-step
samplers. Additionally, with the reversed trigger, we propose backdoor
detection from the noise space, introducing the first backdoor input detection
approach for diffusion models and a novel model detection algorithm that
calculates the KL divergence between reversed and benign distributions.
Extensive evaluations demonstrate that TERD secures a 100% True Positive Rate
(TPR) and True Negative Rate (TNR) across datasets of varying resolutions. TERD
also demonstrates nice adaptability to other Stochastic Differential Equation
(SDE)-based models. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-ML/TERD.
add_method_texts.main_contributions: The paper introduces TERD, a novel backdoor defense framework for diffusion models. TERD provides a unified modeling approach for existing backdoor attacks, enabling the derivation of a reversed loss. It incorporates a trigger reversion strategy and introduces a backdoor detection method in the noise space, including input and model detection algorithms using KL divergence. The framework demonstrates high true positive and negative rates across various datasets and adaptability to SDE-based models.
add_method_texts.methodology: TERD employs a two-stage trigger reversion process: initial trigger estimation using noise from a prior distribution, followed by refinement via differential multi-step samplers. Backdoor detection is performed in the noise space, comparing the distributions of reversed triggers and benign inputs using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence.
add_method_texts.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted on CIFAR-10, CelebA, and CelebA-HQ datasets. The defense was evaluated against BadDiffusion, TrojDiff, and VillanDiffusion attacks. Performance was measured using L2 norm between reversed and original triggers, True Positive Rate (TPR), and True Negative Rate (TNR).
add_method_texts.limitations: The paper does not explicitly state the limitations of the proposed approach. However, the adaptive attack experiments show a degradation in performance when the scaling factor η is extremely low for TrojDiff, suggesting a potential vulnerability when the benign and backdoor distributions have a large overlap.
add_method_texts.future_research_directions: The paper suggests that TERD, including trigger reversion and backdoor detection, can serve as a foundation for improving backdoor robustness in diffusion models. Further research could explore the scalability of TERD to more complex diffusion architectures and investigate defenses against adaptive attacks that more effectively blend benign and backdoor distributions.

base_experimental_code:
The core code for SilentBadDiffusion is found in `src/poisoning_data_generation.py`. It implements the logic for dissecting copyrighted images, generating poisoning images, and assessing similarity. Relevant functions include:

*   `SilentBadDiffusion.forward()`: Orchestrates the poisoning data generation process.
*   `SilentBadDiffusion._init_models()`: Initializes the GroundingDINO, SAM, and inpainting models.
*   `utils.detect()`: Detects objects in images.
*   `utils.segment()`: Performs semantic segmentation.
*   `utils.generate_image()`: Generates images using diffusion inpainting.
`src/composition_attack_load_dataset.py` contains code for loading and preprocessing the datasets, including:
* `load_target_and_poisoning_data()`: Loads both the target (copyrighted) and poisoning data.
* `preprocess_train_silentbaddiffusion()`: Preprocesses training data, including tokenizing captions and shuffling phrases.
`src/target_model_training.py` shows how the target model is fine-tuned using the generated poisoned data. Relevant snippets include:
*   The training loop within `main()`.
*   Configuration of the Stable Diffusion pipeline.
*   The image generation process during validation in `SilentBadDiffusion_validation()`.
base_experimental_info:
The experimental settings are primarily described in `src/target_model_training.py` through command-line arguments handled by `argparse`. These settings include:

*   Dataset selection (`--dataset_name`, `--clean_dataset_name`)
*   Poisoning ratio (`--poisoning_ratio`)
*   Number of few-shot examples (`--n_few_shot`)
*   Target image IDs (`--target_start_id`, `--target_num`)
*   Training parameters (e.g., `--train_batch_size`, `--num_train_epochs`, `--learning_rate`)
*   Inference parameters (`--num_sample_steps`, `--guidance_scale`)
*   Model architecture (`--model_card`)
*   The script also shows the use of Stable Diffusion v1.5, controlled via the `--pretrained_model_name_or_path` argument, and the use of the AdamW optimizer. The datasets used are specified with command line arguments such as `dataset_name` and `clean_dataset_name`.
new_method:
Below is an illustrative example of a genuinely new method (Step 3), drawn from combining insights of the Base Method and a key strategy in the Add Method. This proposed approach aims to address several identified shortcomings of the Base Method while leveraging TERD’s backdoor-detection insights from noise space. Note that the description below focuses on the novel method itself, as requested.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
■ A NOVEL METHOD: DUAL-SPACE DISENTANGLEMENT AND REVERSION (DSDR)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) Core Idea
DSDR tackles silent backdoor embedding (as in SilentBadDiffusion) by jointly:
• Disentangling copyrighted elements in the semantic (image) space, inspired by the Base Method’s decomposition strategy.  
• Applying a trigger reversion mechanism (inspired by TERD) at a latent-noise level to suppress or detect illicit triggers before they become active in generation.

2) Two-Stage Embed-and-Revert Framework

(a) Dual-Space Disentanglement
• Semantic Decomposition: Similar to SilentBadDiffusion, copyrighted images are split into salient components (foreground, stylistic cues, etc.). However, instead of scattering these parts trivially across multiple training images, DSDR encodes each copyright fragment into a paired noise token (latent embedding).  
• Latent Anchoring: Each semantic fragment is mapped to a unique noise “signature” using an encoder. This signature is not merely a small patch but an imperceptible pattern distributed across the latent representation. By doing so, any attempt to leverage these fragments during inference relies on decoding from a concealed noise signature rather than a straightforward visual patch.

(b) Trigger Reversion and Monitoring
• Noise-Space Reconstruction: During inference, suspect prompts are tested by “reverse sampling” a small batch of images from Gaussian noise to see if any embedded signature (associated with known copyrighted fragments) reappears.  
• KL-Divergence–Guided Reversion: If the reversed noise distribution strays too far from a model’s normal, benign distribution, DSDR applies a multi-step noise reversion (similar to TERD). This process incrementally corrects the noise to steer generations away from re-triggering the copyrighted content.  
• Continuous Monitoring: DSDR keeps an online record of approximated noise signatures for each batch. Whenever an outlier distribution consistent with known triggers is detected (based on KL divergence), the system “pushes” those noise embeddings back toward benign territory. This prevents a latent signature from fully activating the copyrighted material.

3) Advantages/Novelty
• Goes Beyond Simple Poisoning: Unlike standard backdoor attacks, where triggers are visible or based on direct pixel-level modifications, DSDR weaves triggers into the noise space. It thus makes backdoor attempts more elusive—but at the same time, the integrated reversion module constantly monitors latent variables for suspicious outliers, thwarting activation.  
• Works Even for Complex or Non-Decomposable Images: By separating the encoding of partial image semantics (foreground, style) from the latent noise signature, DSDR handles both easily decomposable and more complex images. When images are less neatly segmented, the noise-based anchor still carries the key signature.  
• Unified Detection-Prevention Pipeline: Instead of dealing with backdoor detection and remedy as separate modules, DSDR bonds them together. Identification of suspicious triggers is directly followed by noise-space correction, making the pipeline more robust and less prone to “lag” between detection and response.

4) Potential Extensions
• Adaptive Reversion Thresholds: One could fine-tune the KL divergence boundary to dynamically adapt based on the complexity of the training data or the model’s architecture.  
• Multi-Modal Integration: DSDR can incorporate additional signals (e.g., from an audio or textual domain) to refine detection of suspicious cross-modal triggers, broadening relevance to more general generative tasks.  
• Watermarking for Forensic Tracking: By appending a benign watermark to all outputs unless triggered noise reversion kicks in, auditors can easily flag outputs that bypassed DSDR, further discouraging malicious usage.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OUTCOME OF STEP 3
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Dual-Space Disentanglement and Reversion (DSDR) is a truly new method that combines the Base Method’s semantic fragmentation of copyrighted content with a noise-based trigger reversion mechanism akin to TERD. By integrating a dedicated noise-space monitoring and reversion process, DSDR addresses the Base Method’s vulnerabilities—such as limited detection of stealthy poisoned content and over-reliance on a single similarity measure—while offering more comprehensive protection against backdoor attacks and copyright infringements.
